items.title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
items.text: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. items.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
items.text: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. items.title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
items.text: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. items.text: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. items.text: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. items.text: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). items.title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?
items.text: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.

items.title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
items.text: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

items.title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
items.text: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements

items.text: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. items.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
items.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

items.text: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. items.title: Decoding Transformer Dynamics via Koopman Subspaces
items.text: We apply Koopman operator theory and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to characterise how large language models (LLMs) process different input topics. Treating the layer-to-layer evolution of hidden states as a dynamical system, we fit a linear Koopman operator and take the subspace spanned by its dominant modes as a per-topic spectral fingerprint. Four findings emerge. First, the depth map is near-linear: a single linear operator predicts each next-layer state to within approx. 18% relative error (interior variance explained approx. 0.99). Second, over the 57 MMLU subjects the fingerprint is topic-discriminative, matching the MMLU taxonomy at 0.72 nearest-neighbour purity and each subject's semantic neighbourhood at 0.75 any-hit@3. Third, it is a reproducible signature (split-half self-retrieval approx. 0.97$). Finally, these findings are consistent across seven base models (Qwen2.5 0.5-7B, Llama-3 1-8B), with a suggestive trend of alignment rising with MMLU accuracy. The spectral fingerprint thus provides a probe of how transformers process different topics across depth. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepK/koopman-llm-eacl27.

items.title: LoopSeek: Decoupling System One Search from System Two Answering for Long Video Understanding
items.text: Long video question answering requires finding relevant evidence before reasoning over it. With a limited frame budget, single-pass frame selection can miss critical evidence, while adaptive search often relies on repeated text generation to decide where to look. We introduce LoopSeek, a framework that decouples evidence search from answer generation through a division of labor between a non-thinking System I and a generative System II. Our key insight is that search can be expressed as a sequence of small, typed decisions, allowing System I to find the evidence that System II needs. Four System I role agents navigate a tree of video windows and coordinate through probability outputs to select frames, assess evidence, and revise the search without generating text. To align search with System II, System I learns from annotated evidence on questions that System II answers correctly only from that evidence, and the verifier's evidence estimates steer the search without calling System II, which stays frozen and answers once from the selected frames. items.title: CLASP: Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling for Zero-Shot OOD Detection using Vision-Language Models
items.text: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in medical imaging, yet existing approaches often rely on final-layer confidence or entropy-based layer selection, potentially missing complementary information. We show that low in-distribution (ID) confidence entropy does not reliably predict OOD discrimination. We introduce CLASP (Complementary Layer Selection and Profiling), an ID-only framework that jointly models layer--prompt responses and visual features. CLASP ranks visual encoder layers using Gaussian conditional mutual information and selects a compact subset through anchored spectral selection, without fixing the number of layers. It then combines the selected layer--prompt profiles with PCA-compressed visual embeddings and fits a single shrinkage-regularized Gaussian. OOD scores are computed using squared Mahalanobis distance, without fine-tuning, OOD training data, or test-time adaptation. Across histopathology, chest X-ray, and brain MRI benchmarks with UniMedCLIP and BioMedCLIP, CLASP performs strongly under varied distribution shifts. On MIDOG near-OOD, it achieves 87.54% AUROC with UniMedCLIP, outperforming confidence-based baseline

items.title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity
items.text: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. items.title: Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
items.text: Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. items.title: Who Speaks for the Water? Simulating Discursive Closure and Power Asymmetries in Hydrosocial Governance
items.text: Water governance conflicts stem not only from material scarcity, but from power asymmetries, institutional distrust, and the discursive frameworks through which actors assign meaning to water, infrastructure, and legitimate authority. Conventional simulation tools represent these dynamics via numerical opinion variables, missing the argumentative and narrative dimensions structuring real deliberation in hydrosocial territories. We present the Hydrosocial Agent-Based Model with Large Language Models (HSABM-LLM), a hybrid framework enabling heterogeneous agents to generate, evaluate, and adapt natural language arguments conditioned on institutional roles, interaction histories, and territorial context. Grounded in semi-structured interviews, a water-user survey, and 456 press and official documents from the Longaví River sub-basin (Maule Region, Chile), the model simulates deliberation over a contested large-scale reservoir proposal across four experimental scenarios. Opinion convergence toward unanimous opposition emerged within 7-14 months, operating through discursive closure driven by distributive equity and water security framings rather than argumentative dominance. items.title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
items.text: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. items.text:
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀.



It is teaching them to stop flattening people into language names.



“Arabic.”

“English.”

“Spanish.”

...



These labels are convenient for datasets.



But humans do not speak labels.



We speak from cities, villages, families, histories, professions, memories, migrations, jokes, wounds, rituals, and relationships.



A grandmother does not speak like a government form.



A patient does not describe pain like a Wikipedia article.



A farmer, a nurse, a student, a shopkeeper, a traveler, and a child do not all speak the same “standard” version of a language.



And yet, much of modern AI still behaves as if language were  uniform, and separable from the people who use it.



This is one of the great unsolved problems in multilingual AI.



Not only translation.



𝗩𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴.

𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁.

𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿.

𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁.

𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆.



This is the global problem behind our new project:

𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮.



The name is intentional.



Alexandria was never just a city.



It was one of humanity’s boldest symbols of knowledge moving across languages, cultures, and worlds.



A place where translation was not clerical work.

It was civilization-building.



Today, we borrow that name for a new question at the heart of AI:



𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀?



For too long, Arabic has been flattened in technology.



One label: “Arabic.”

One assumed standard.

One imagined speaker.

One simplified linguistic reality.



But Arabic is not one voice.



Arabic is Cairo and Casablanca.



Amman and Muscat.

Khartoum and Tunis.

Beirut and Riyadh.

Sana’a, Tripoli, Nouakchott, Gaza, Damascus, Algiers, Doha, Manama, and beyond.



It is dialect.

It is register.

It is gendered interaction.

It is code-switching.

It is place, intimacy, politeness, humor, memory, identity, and everyday life.



So I am thrilled to share that 𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮 has been accepted to 𝗔𝗖𝗟 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗠𝗮𝗶𝗻.



𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮: 𝗔 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗜𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀



Alexandria is our largest community-built Arabic machine translation project so far: a large-scale, human-translated, multi-domain dataset designed to help AI systems translate Arabic as people actually use it.



It brings together:

📷 𝟭𝟯 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀

📷 𝟯𝟰𝗞+ 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

📷 𝟭𝟬𝟳𝗞+ 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵 📷 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝘀

📷 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿–𝗮𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

📷 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗼𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲-𝘀𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵, 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗦𝗔

📷 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗴𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 to support reproducibility and future community work



But Alexandria is not only a dataset.



It is a refusal.



A refusal to treat dialects as noise.



A refusal to treat “standard” language as the only legitimate language.



A refusal to build AI systems that understand the center and mishear the margins.



Dialects are not broken versions of languages.

They are knowledge systems.



They carry social meaning.

They carry identity.

They carry memory.

They carry belonging.

They carry the subtle difference between being translated and being understood.



When AI erases dialects, it does not merely make a linguistic mistake.



It erases context.

It erases communities.

It erases the conditions under which language becomes human.



Our findings show a clear gap: current LLMs can often preserve meaning reasonably well, but still struggle to generate fluent, locally authentic dialectal Arabic, especially across fine-grained sub-dialects, domains, and social contexts.



That gap matters.



It matters when a patient describes symptoms in the words that feel natural to them.



It matters when a farmer asks for advice.

It matters when a student learns.

It matters when a traveler seeks help.

It matters when public services are supposed to reach everyone, not only those who speak the “right” variety.



Alexandria is our attempt to say something plainly:



𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘀.



We need systems that can handle variation, not erase it.

Systems that can model culture, not smooth it away.

Systems that understand that linguistic diversity is not a complication to be removed.



It is the world.



This is true for Arabic.



It is also true globally, for languages with dialects, accents, registers, contact varieties, mixed codes, regional forms, Indigenous varieties, diasporic forms, youth speech, professional speech, and deeply situated cultural meanings.



In the old Alexandria, knowledge moved across languages.



With this new Alexandria, we hope to help AI move across dialects, communities, and lived realities.

items.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
items.text: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. items.text: Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. items.title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
items.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.

items.title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World
items.text: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

items.text: Looped transformers do not acquire new knowledge during a forward pass. Prior work shows that they store as many bits in their weights as non-looped models. items.text: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. items.title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
items.text: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. To address these, we introduce a forecasting training framework including harness design and post-training. For the harness side, we propose Proactive Belief-State Management (PBM), equipping agents with a fold tool to compress lengthy context into compact belief states and reset the context for subsequent exploration. For the training side, we develop SEIPH, a five-dimensional, outcome-blind rubric, providing process-quality rewards. Using the rubric-based reward, we post-train a 35B model with PPO and GRPO, yielding DeepForecaster-PPO and DeepForecaster-GRPO. Theoretically, we prove that idealized fold-based stopping converges and calibrated local rewards reduce segment-level gradient variance. Empirically, DeepForecaster-PPO (35B) achieves the best Brier score on both ForecastBench and Polymarket-Sim, outperforming frontier agents
